title: Indifference
hook: not coldness but freedom: not preferring health to sickness, wealth to poverty, for their own sake

segments.voice: Yesterday, the principle and foundation: made to praise, reverence and serve God, and everything else used as it helps. Your line was as far as it helps. What did you hold up to the question? Day one thousand one hundred forty.

Call someone indifferent today and it's an insult. It means they don't care. The shrug, the blank text back, the person who walks past. So it's a jolt to find the word sitting right in the middle of Ignatius's Spiritual Exercises as something to want. In the same paragraph as yesterday's foundation, he says we need to make ourselves indifferent to all created things. Not wanting health more than sickness. Not riches more than poverty. Not honor more than dishonor, or a long life more than a short one. Taken one way, that sounds cold, even inhuman. Ignatius means nearly the opposite. Today's word: indifference.

The key is that none of these things is wanted for its own sake, and Ignatius limits it to what is left to our free choice and not forbidden. He isn't saying sickness is as good as health, or that nobody should look after a body or pay the rent. He's saying don't let any one of those things own you. If you need to be healthy, rich and admired no matter what, then those needs make your choices for you. You aren't free. Indifference, for Ignatius, is balance: standing like a scale that hasn't tipped yet, so that the only weight that tips it is what God is asking, what serves love. Then comes the second half of his sentence, which is all desire. We should want and choose only what helps us toward the end we're made for. So indifference isn't wanting nothing. It's wanting one thing so much that everything else can move. Paul writes from prison, in his letter to the Philippians: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound." Learned, notice. Not born with it. And a Gospel scene fits the same shape: Jesus in the garden the night before he dies. He doesn't pretend he wants the cross. He asks for the cup to pass. And then: "nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt." That's not coldness. It's freedom, and a warm kind: a real preference, said out loud, and then held open.
screen: `NOT AS I WILL, BUT AS THOU WILT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold one preference loosely. Sit and breathe. Choose something you're hoping for right now: a result, a reply, a plan going your way. Let yourself want it honestly. Don't pretend you don't. Then picture both outcomes, the one you want and the other one, and see whether love could still be found in the second. If you pray, you can say the line from the garden, not as I will, but as thou wilt, and mean only as much of it as you can. If you don't, just let the hope sit beside the other outcome, both in view. The bell holds the time.
Indifference. In Ignatius, not coldness but freedom: wanting nothing created for its own sake, so you're free to choose what serves God and love.
Your line: free to choose love. Today, when something doesn't go your way, before you react, ask what love would choose from here. Day one thousand one hundred forty.

howItsDone: In Ignatian spirituality, people making a decision pray first for indifference, the inner freedom to choose whatever best serves God, often with a spiritual director, before weighing the options.

pairs: a scale that hasn't tipped yet
not as I will, but as thou wilt

myth: it means not being owned by any created thing, so you're free to choose love.
the same sentence goes on: want and choose only what helps toward the end we're made for.
in the garden, Jesus says he wants the cross
he asks for the cup to pass, then says not as I will, but as thou wilt.

fork.setup: you're praying over a decision you care a lot about. what does Ignatius ask first?
options: pretend you don't have a preference.
name your preference, then hold it open so love can tip the scale.
pick the harder option, since it must be holier.
fork.reveal: indifference isn't faking. it's a real preference held loosely, the way Jesus in the garden asks for the cup to pass and then says not as I will.

original.note: Greek: content, having enough within; Paul's word in Philippians 4:11.

trapdoor: what you thought: indifference means not caring.
what it means: in Ignatius, a freedom that wants nothing created for its own sake, so love can choose.
what a scholar hears: §23 of the Exercises pairs being indifferent to health, wealth, honor and length of life with desiring only what leads to our end.
recall: the Russian name for a prayer rope

notes: Spiritual Exercises §23 paraphrased: indifference to health/sickness, riches/poverty, honor/dishonor, long life/short life; then 'desiring and choosing only what is most conducive for us to the end for which we are created'. Confirm.
'Standing like a scale that hasn't tipped' draws on Ignatius's image of the balance (Exercises §179); confirm the image is fair here.
'Paul writes from prison' rests on Philippians 1:13 (bonds); confirm phrasing.
Original: αὐτάρκης (Philippians 4:11), gloss 'content, having enough within'; confirm accent and pronunciation.
